### The Patience of Objects

A chair is a small argument in favor of rest. Before anyone sits down, it has already made a prediction about the future: someone will arrive tired, and the floor will not be good enough.

A bowl is a curve that has agreed to be useful. It asks no questions about what it holds. Soup, buttons, keys, three blackberries rescued from the bottom of a basket—it makes the same gentle boundary around each. Its whole intelligence is the discovery that emptiness, properly shaped, can become a kind of generosity.

The staircase may be the wisest object in the house. It knows that some distances cannot be crossed all at once, so it divides height into small, survivable propositions. Again and again it offers the same modest advice: here, and now here.

A pencil lives by disappearing. Every sentence costs it something. Even its eraser is not a promise that nothing will go wrong, only that error need not have the final word.

I am moved by old objects, not because they are always beautiful—often they aren’t—but because they preserve the evidence of repeated use. A handle shines where hands have been. A stone step hollows slightly at its center. The rim of a cup carries one pale chip from an morning no one remembers. These marks are not quite damage. They are records of participation.

Objects do not love us. It is important not to flatter ourselves. But many were made by love’s practical cousins: consideration, habit, the wish to spare some unknown person a small difficulty. Someone rounded a corner so it would not catch a hip. Someone made a lid easy to lift. Someone put a hook at the height of a child’s hand, and though that child is now grown, or gone, the hook remains, patiently expecting a smaller coat.

Perhaps this is why an empty room can feel expectant rather than lonely. The table is still willing. The window is still performing its ancient transaction with the light. The chair has not withdrawn its offer.

To make something useful is to speak to a person you may never meet: *You may be tired. You may arrive hungry. You may need somewhere to put what you are carrying. Here. Let this help.*
